{{Short description|Circle associated with any given triangle}}
[[File:Van Lamoen circle.svg|thumb|right|400px| The van Lamoen circle through six circumcenters <math>A_b</math>, <math>A_c</math>, <math> B_c</math>, <math>B_a</math>, <math>C_a</math>, <math>C_b</math>]]

In [[Euclidean plane]] [[geometry]], the '''van Lamoen circle''' is a special [[circle]] associated with any given [[triangle]] <math>T</math>.  It contains the [[circumcenter]]s of the six triangles that are defined inside <math>T</math> by its three [[median (geometry)|median]]s.<ref name=kimberlingX1153/><ref name=wolframVLC/>

Specifically, let <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, <math>C</math> be the [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]] of <math>T</math>, and let <math>G</math> be its [[centroid]] (the intersection of its three medians).  Let <math>M_a</math>, <math>M_b</math>, and <math>M_c</math> be the midpoints of the sidelines <math>BC</math>, <math>CA</math>, and <math>AB</math>, respectively. It turns out that the circumcenters of the six triangles <math>AGM_c</math>, <math>BGM_c</math>, <math> BGM_a</math>, <math>CGM_a</math>, <math>CGM_b</math>, and <math>AGM_b</math> lie on a common circle, which is the van Lamoen circle of <math>T</math>.<ref name=wolframVLC/>

==History==

The van Lamoen circle is named after the mathematician {{ill|Floor van Lamoen|nl}} who posed it as a problem in 2000.<ref name=lamoen2000/><ref name=liVLC/> A proof was provided by [[Kin Y. Li]] in 2001,<ref name=liVLC/> and the editors of the Amer. Math. Monthly in 2002.<ref name=kimberlingX1153/><ref name=lamoen2002/>

==Properties==

The center of the van Lamoen circle is point <math>X(1153)</math> in [[Clark Kimberling]]'s [[Kimberling center|comprehensive list]] of [[triangle center]]s.<ref name=kimberlingX1153/>

In 2003, [[Alexey Myakishev]] and [[Peter Y. Woo]] proved that the converse of the theorem is nearly true, in the following sense: let <math>P</math> be any point in the triangle's interior, and <math>AA'</math>, <math>BB'</math>, and <math>CC'</math> be its [[cevian]]s, that is, the [[line segment]]s that connect each vertex to <math>P</math> and are extended until each meets the opposite side.  Then the circumcenters of the six triangles <math>APB'</math>, <math>APC'</math>, <math>BPC'</math>, <math> BPA'</math>, <math>CPA'</math>, and <math>CPB'</math> lie on the same circle if and only if <math>P</math> is the centroid of <math>T</math> or its [[orthocenter]] (the intersection of its three [[altitude (triangle)|altitudes]]), at which point the six circumcenters degenerate into the three Euler points of the [[nine-point circle]].<ref name=makwooVLC/>  A simpler proof of this result was given by [[Nguyen Minh Ha]] in 2005.<ref name=haVLC/>
